answer:
**Training needs feedback about how to improve, not just whether the current answer is wrong.** Zero-one loss is flat while a prediction stays on the same side of a decision boundary. A tiny parameter change usually leaves it unchanged, so its local gradient gives no useful direction. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

Cross-entropy distinguishes a correct answer at probability 0.51 from one at 0.99, and a wrong answer at 0.49 from one at 0.001. For a binary logit z, its derivative is $\sigma(z)-y$. A confidently wrong positive example gives a strong negative derivative, pushing the logit upward.

**The surrogate is easier to optimize, but it is not the final product metric.** Logistic loss is convex for linear logits; adding a neural network generally removes that convexity. Exact zero-one optimization difficulty also depends on the hypothesis class, so an unqualified complexity slogan is misleading.

Train with a suitable differentiable objective, then choose thresholds and evaluate costs, accuracy, or ranking on independent data. A well-optimized log loss does not automatically select the threshold needed for an asymmetric decision problem.

**Technical details and references.**

Zero-one loss changes only when a prediction crosses the decision boundary, so it gives no useful local gradient almost everywhere and creates a difficult discontinuous optimization problem. Cross-entropy provides a smooth probability-sensitive surrogate. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

For binary logits, its gradient is $\sigma(z)-y$, giving a strong correction for confidently wrong examples. Convexity holds for linear logits, not arbitrary neural networks. Minimizing log loss does not directly optimize every downstream threshold/cost metric, so select thresholds and evaluate accuracy/utility separately. The difficulty of exact zero-one minimization depends on the hypothesis class; avoid a universal complexity claim without specifying it.
